explanation:
## Four lines

```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
  if (rst)     q <= '0;
  else if (en) q <= q + 1'b1;
end
```

and every part of it is load-bearing.

**`@(posedge clk)` and nothing else.** The sensitivity list of a synchronous design names the clock and, if the reset is asynchronous, the reset. This reset is synchronous, so it is not in the list — it is tested *inside* the block, which is what makes it take effect only when an edge arrives.

**`<=`, not `=`.** Non-blocking assignment. All the right-hand sides in the design are evaluated with the values the registers held *before* the edge, and then every left-hand side is updated. That is what makes a clock edge a single simultaneous event rather than a sequence, and it is why `a <= b; b <= a;` swaps two registers while `a = b; b = a;` sets both to the old `b`.

**No `else`.** A register with no assignment on this edge keeps its value, which is exactly "hold". Writing `else q <= q;` is the same thing at more length.

**Wrapping is free.** `q + 1` on an N-bit vector is N-bit arithmetic, so all-ones plus one is zero. There is nothing to write, and the attempts to write it are where the bugs are: `if (q == 15)` is wrong for any N but 4, and `q <= (q + 1) % N` confuses the width with the modulus.

## What the grading testbench finds

Three bugs that pass every visible check.

**Saturating instead of wrapping.** `if (q != {N{1'b1}}) q <= q + 1;` counts to 15 and stops. The sample testbench never goes past 3.

**Enable beating reset.** `if (en) q <= q + 1; else if (rst) q <= 0;` reads naturally and has the priority backwards. The sample testbench never raises both, so it never notices. A real reset has to work whatever else is happening — that is what it is for.

**An asynchronous reset where a synchronous one was asked for.** `always_ff @(posedge clk or posedge rst)` responds to the reset immediately rather than at the next edge. The `sync_reset` check raises and lowers `rst` entirely between two clock edges: a synchronous design does not notice, and an asynchronous one clears.

Which of the two you want is a real design decision rather than a preference. Asynchronous reset works with no clock running, which matters at power-on; synchronous reset is easier to time and cannot produce a reset release that violates recovery time. Most designs use asynchronous assert and synchronous release, which is a third thing again. The exercise asks for synchronous because that is what the specification says, and a design that does something else is not the design that was asked for.

## Reading it off the waveform

Put the cursor just after a rising edge and `q` has the new value; just before, the old one. That gap is the non-blocking update, and it is why both testbenches read `q` at `@(negedge clk)` rather than straight after the `@(posedge clk)` they waited for. A testbench that samples on the same edge the design uses is reading a race, and it is the commonest testbench bug there is.

Simulation only: none of this says the design would synthesise or meet timing.
